issues.description: Omission of key demographic covariates: The cross-lagged model only includes SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice, without adjusting for critical demographic and socioeconomic covariates. Variables such as age, gender, education, income, and baseline political affiliation are known to strongly influence both ideological orientations (SDO/RWA) and environmental attitudes. By omitting these covariates, the observed longitudinal associations may be spurious and driven by these unmodeled confounding factors. The authors should include these standard demographic variables as covariates in their model to demonstrate that the predictive power of SDO and RWA holds over and above these foundational differences.

issues.description: Unjustified causal inference: The authors rely on a standard cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) to infer a causal relationship, but standard CLPMs are known to confound between-person differences (trait-like stability) with within-person fluctuations. This makes causal claims based on these models highly problematic, as the lagged paths may simply reflect unmodeled between-person variance rather than true within-person developmental processes. To better support claims of directional influence, the authors should employ a Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM) to separate within-person variance from between-person variance. Furthermore, observational longitudinal data cannot definitively establish causality without accounting for all unmeasured confounders. I recommend re-analyzing the data using an RI-CLPM and softening the causal language throughout the manuscript to reflect the observational nature of the data.

issues.description: Narrow operationalization of environmentalism: The study operationalizes the broad construct of "environmentalism" using only two items focused specifically on the willingness to make personal and financial sacrifices. While sacrifice is an important component of pro-environmental behavior, it is heavily confounded with personal wealth, economic security, and disposable income—factors that also intersect with social dominance and hierarchy. Equating "willingness to sacrifice" with general "environmentalism" or "climate change denial" overstates the scope of the dependent variable. The authors should explicitly acknowledge this narrow operationalization as a limitation and temper their generalizations, ensuring that conclusions specifically reference "willingness to make environmental sacrifices" rather than broad environmentalism.

issues.description: Unaddressed cross-cultural generalizability limits: While the use of a nationally representative New Zealand sample is a methodological strength, the manuscript lacks a discussion of how New Zealand's specific socio-political and environmental context might limit the generalizability of the findings to other nations. New Zealand has unique political dynamics, indigenous relations, and environmental policies that may uniquely shape the intersection of social dominance, authoritarianism, and environmental attitudes. The authors should contextualize these findings within the broader international literature and explicitly address potential limits to cross-cultural generalizability.

issues.description: Vague future research directions: The suggestion to use qualitative methods to probe the rationale behind environmental attitudes is somewhat generic and disconnected from the specific theoretical mechanisms discussed earlier in the text. A more targeted and actionable future direction would be to propose empirical tests of the specific mechanisms highlighted in the discussion, such as experimental studies examining whether framing environmental action as hierarchy-enhancing (rather than hierarchy-attenuating) causally alters the pro-environmental behavioral intentions of high-SDO individuals.

issues.description: Disconnect in environmental racism literature: The discussion of environmental racism and inequality relies heavily on literature that is predominantly situated in the United States. Given that the empirical data is drawn entirely from New Zealand, the manuscript would benefit from integrating literature on environmental inequality specific to the New Zealand context, such as the disproportionate environmental impacts on Māori communities. Bridging this gap would better align the theoretical framework of environmental inequality with the actual sample population being studied.

issues.description: Inadequate justification for poor CFI: The authors report a Comparative Fit Index (CFI) of 0.86, which falls below the widely accepted threshold of 0.90 for acceptable model fit. The justification that CFI is "affected by model complexity" is insufficient, as CFI compares the target model to a baseline null model and a low value often indicates substantial misspecification in the measurement or structural model. The authors should either respecify the model to achieve acceptable fit across multiple indices, or provide a much more robust methodological justification for accepting a model with a CFI of 0.86.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: Unclear handling of missing indicator: The authors state that one of the RWA items was not assessed at time two, yet they also report constraining factor loadings and residual variances to equality across all five time points. It is mathematically unclear how the factor loading and residual variance for this specific item were constrained at time two when the item itself was not administered. The authors must explicitly detail the parameterization used in Mplus to handle this structural missingness while maintaining the stationary model constraints, ensuring that the latent RWA construct remains strictly comparable across all waves.

issues.description: Unreported attrition and missing data: The manuscript relies on a five-year longitudinal sample of 22,974 participants and uses Full Information Maximum Likelihood (FIML) to handle missing data. However, the authors do not report the attrition rate across the five waves, nor do they describe the patterns of missingness. In large multi-year panel studies, attrition is often substantial and non-random. Because FIML assumes data are Missing At Random (MAR), the authors must report the proportion of missing data at each time point and provide analyses evaluating whether attrition is systematically related to the baseline variables (SDO, RWA, or environmentalism).

Impossible chi-square difference value: The text reports a chi-square difference of 15,389.13 for the test comparing the lagged effect of RWA on SDO (B = .02, SD = .003) and SDO on RWA (B = -.001, SD = .01). Given the small magnitude of these coefficients and their standard errors, a chi-square value of over 15,000 is mathematically impossible (the Z-score for the difference is approximately 2, which would yield a chi-square around 4). This is likely a typographical error (e.g., for 15.389) that drastically misrepresents the magnitude of the statistical test.

issues.description: Contradictory direction of strongest lagged effect: In the Results section, the text states that "the lagged effect on SDO was stronger than the reverse", which refers to the effect of environmentalism on SDO (B = -.04). However, the very next sentence concludes that "SDO has a stonger influence on environmental attitudes over time than the reverse", which refers to the effect of SDO on environmentalism (B = -.11). The coefficient for SDO on environmentalism (-.11) is indeed larger in magnitude than the reverse (-.04), meaning the first sentence incorrectly states that the effect *on* SDO was stronger (likely a typo for the effect *of* SDO).
